extracted.intended_audience: patent and trademark practitioners, USPTO respondents, and attorneys facing OED disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used by the USPTO (and its adjudicatory body) to determine whether a person has engaged in unauthorized practice before the Office or other disciplinary misconduct in patent and trademark matters. Covers definitions of practice, applicable rules, required state of mind, jurisdictional questions, and evidentiary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'practice before the Office' in patent matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice before the Office in patent matters includes, but is not limited to, preparing and prosecuting any patent application; consulting with or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing a patent application or other document with the Office; drafting the specification or claims of a patent application; drafting an amendment or reply to a communication from the Office that may require written argument to establish the patentability of a claimed invention; drafting a reply to a communication from the Office regarding a patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1). The Court found drafting patent applications, drafting responses to Office Actions, and advising clients on patentability are acts that constitute practice before the Office. Mere transcription of a client's words may not constitute practice, but rephrasing or adding legal analysis does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'practice before the Office' in trademark matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice before the Office in trademark matters includes consulting with or giving advice to a client in contemplation of filing a trademark application or other document with the Office; preparing and prosecuting an application for trademark registration; conducting an appeal to the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(2). Filing and prosecuting trademark applications and participating before the TTAB constitute practice before the Office and bring the actor within USPTO disciplinary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is a 'practitioner' and applicability of disciplinary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'practitioner' means an individual authorized under 5 U.S.C. 500(b), or otherwise as provided by § 11.14(a),(b),(c) to practice before the Office. Practitioners are subject to the USPTO disciplinary rules; even persons not registered may be subject to discipline if they provide or offer to provide legal services before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.1, 11.14, 11.19. The regulation states that a person not registered who provides or offers to provide legal services before the Office is subject to disciplinary authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized practice of law before the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Only practitioners registered under § 11.6 are permitted to prosecute patent applications of others before the Office or represent others in any proceedings before the Office; representing or providing the types of services defined as practice before the Office when not authorized constitutes unauthorized practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.6, 11.10, 11.5, and case law (e.g., In re Amalgamated Dev. Co., In re Herren). Advising inventors on patentability, preparing patent applications (including specifications and claims), and preparing and filing amendments are examples of practicing law. Distinction: pure typing/transcription may be permissible; adding legal rephrasing/opinion is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on practicing law in violation of jurisdictional rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners may not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of the regulation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction; the USPTO is considered 'another jurisdiction' for purposes of such rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.505 and precedent (e.g., In re Kenneth Paul Campbell). Unauthorized practice before the USPTO can be considered misconduct under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 11.116 — not representing if representation will violate USPTO rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not represent a client if doing so will result in a violation of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the requested representation would result in unauthorized practice before the Office (or other violations), acceptance or provision of that representation violates § 11.116.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) (2012) and 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c). Deceit is defined as behavior meant to fool; misrepresentation includes false or misleading assertions by words or conduct; concealment or non-disclosure may amount to misrepresentation. The OED must prove such misconduct by clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: False or misleading communications about practitioner or services
rubrics_metrics.description: A communication is false or misleading if it contains a material misrepresentation of fact or law, or omits a fact necessary to make the statement considered as a whole not materially misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.701. This rule does not appear to require intent or knowledge — making an objectively false or materially misleading statement can violate the rule. Example: telling a client the USPTO 'would not enforce' rules about pro se filings when that is misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct which impedes or subverts the process of resolving disputes, or frustrates the fair balance of interests or 'justice' essential to litigation or other proceedings, is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) (2012) and 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d), and case law. Unauthorized practice of law is treated as a serious threat to the effective administration of justice and can constitute this misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal acts reflecting adversely on honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Commission of a criminal act that reflects adversely on a practitioner's honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness as a practitioner is grounds for discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(b). Example alleged: violation of 35 U.S.C. § 33 (falsely holding oneself out as registered). The decision requires clear and convincing evidence to find such a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to respond to lawful demand for information (RFIs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner, in connection with a disciplinary matter, shall not knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information unless disclosure is protected (e.g., privileged). 'Knowingly' means actual knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b) and § 11.1. Courts note limits to attorney-client privilege (identity of client generally not protected). A general, unsupported claim of privilege (without a privilege log) is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director must establish violations of the USPTO disciplinary rules by clear and convincing evidence in these proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision repeatedly applies the 'clear and convincing' standard when evaluating claims (e.g., dishonesty, criminal acts, misrepresentation). Where evidence is lacking or only shows negligence, the rule may not be found violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of intent/knowledge to different rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Some disciplinary rules require intent or knowledge (e.g., 'knowingly' failing to respond to RFIs), while others (e.g., § 11.701 on false or misleading communications) do not require intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess violations with attention to the mens rea the specific regulation requires; absence of intent may excuse some charges but not others that are strict-liability in effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO's regulatory authority and Chevron deference
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO created its rule regulating authorized practice before the Office through notice-and-comment rulemaking pursuant to its statutory authority and thus is entitled to Chevron deference regarding its interpretation of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 73 Fed. Reg. 47650 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.5; relies on 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) and Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. NRDC. Respondents may challenge the statute's interpretation on appeal but the administrative tribunal follows promulgated regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary jurisdiction extends to trademark filers and non-registered persons
rubrics_metrics.description: All practitioners engaged in practice before the Office are subject to disciplinary jurisdiction; a person not registered is also subject to disciplinary authority if the person provides or offers to provide any legal services before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.1, 11.5(b)(2), 11.19. Misconduct can be disciplined whether or not it occurred in the course of providing legal services or in matters pending before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice via filing system and TMEP; ignorance is not an excuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about who may represent trademark owners and the Standards of Conduct (including discipline) is accessible through the electronic filing system (TEAS) and the Trademark Manual of Examining Procedure (TMEP); practitioners who practice before the Office 'knew or should have known' these contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court noted hyperlinks and TMEP sections that inform filers about representation and disciplinary authority; lack of knowledge or ignorance of USPTO rules is not typically a defense (citing In re Piccone). The Court found it took only a few clicks to find this information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing permissible ministerial assistance from legal practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A pure typing service that merely transcribes information furnished by clients may be legitimately provided by non-attorneys, but rephrasing client statements or adding legal analysis/opinions transforms the activity into the practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Herren and other authorities. Evaluate the substance of the work (did it involve legal rephrasing, opinions, or strategy?) rather than just the label used by the actor.
